observer.intro: This reconstructs the mechanical triage an observer would run over the data on this disk: directory names, timestamps, and a keyword sweep. It is an approximation — a server-side export holds a different slice. What it proves is what is findable here, in seconds, without anyone reading a sentence by hand.
observer.section.projects: What the directory names alone reveal
observer.section.sweep: What a keyword sweep would hit
observer.identity.note: Account metadata, plus per-user session and cost figures in the admin analytics. No content — but it identifies you.
observer.projects.note: Claude Code encodes the working path into the directory name. No file has to be opened for this.
observer.pattern.note: An outlier at 23:00 on a Sunday stands out more the more uniform the rest looks. Noise is not a hiding place — it is the contrast.
observer.pattern.pointer: Start of day, breaks, end of day and the whole timesheet those timestamps add up to are under “{tab}”.
observer.sweep.note: Searching all of it takes seconds. The excerpts below are what an observer would read first.
observer.verdict.clean: A triage today would report: work content only.
observer.verdict.private: A triage would surface private content.
observer.verdict.credentials: A triage would surface credentials — treat those as exposed.
cli.help.observer: show what a triage over the local data would surface
observer.verdict.mentions: A triage would surface topic mentions — check whether any are private.

worktime.intro: Every line a session writes carries a timestamp, to the millisecond. Read in order they stop describing what was worked on and start describing when: start of day, breaks, end of day, the Sunday evening, the hour after midnight. Nobody set up a time clock — one exists anyway. This is that reconstruction, run on the local copy in this machine’s time zone, which is exactly what anyone holding the data could run.
worktime.subtitle: {first} to {last} · {sessions} transcripts · {stamps} timestamps
worktime.method: A minute with at least one event counts as worked. A gap of up to {gap} minutes counts as continued work, a longer one as a break. Days are cut at local midnight, so work past midnight lands on the following day.
worktime.method.floor: It is a lower bound: work without Claude Code leaves no timestamp here, and these are figures for activity, not attendance.
worktime.empty: No timestamps found. Without local transcripts there is nothing to reconstruct — which is also what deleting the history achieves.
worktime.hours.note: Minutes of working time per hour of the day. Bars outside {start}:00–{end}:00 are marked — that window is a convention of this tool, not a rule about your hours.
worktime.weekday.note: Working time per weekday across the whole period.
worktime.weeks.note: {shown} of {total} weeks, most recent last. Weeks above {target} h: {over}.
worktime.weeks.label: Week {week}
worktime.days.note: {shown} of {total} days. Start, end, working time, breaks — a timesheet nobody filled in.
worktime.projects.note: Time attributed per project. A minute in which two projects were open counts for both, so the total can exceed the working time above.
worktime.verdict.empty: Nothing to reconstruct — no local timestamps.
worktime.verdict.business: Start, end and breaks are readable for every day; all of it inside business hours.
worktime.verdict.offhours: Start, end, breaks — and the evenings or weekends stand out as clearly as the rest.
worktime.verdict.both: Start, end, breaks, night work and weekend work — all of it readable to the minute.
worktime.note.clock: This is a time clock nobody agreed to. It runs on data that exists for a different purpose, it needs no configuration, and the same reconstruction is possible for anyone holding a copy — for the local copy, deleting the history under “{tab}” is what ends it.
